newsitem.title: USA: Date set to decide details of Korea talks.
newsitem.headline: Date set to decide details of Korea talks.

text.p: The United States, South Korea and North Korea agreed on Monday to hold four-nation talks in New York on Aug. 5 to prepare for negotiations to replace the armistice that ended the Korean War with a formal treaty.
The meeting will determine the date, venue, agenda and procedures in preparation for the formal start of peace talks, according to a statement by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
A joint statement by the United States, South Korea and North Korea after a day-long senior-level meeting in New York said China would join the August talks.

The proposed four-party negotiations would aim to replace the armistice with a formal peace treaty. The armistice ended the fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War, but technically not the war on the Korean peninsula.

North Korean and South Korean delegation leaders earlier told each other they hoped for good results from the Monday meeting, a follow-up to talks in March and April to discuss a proposal by Washington and Seoul for four-nation talks.

According to a U.S. official, the North Korean delegation leader, Vice Foreign Minister Kim Gye Gwan, said earlier in the day: "Last time we were concerned that there might be a premature baby, but this time we're not concerned about a premature baby."
The South Korean delegation is led by Deputy Foreign Minister Song Yong Shik and the U.S. delegation by Charles Kartman, the acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific Affairs.
Communist North Korea, threatened by famine, agreed in principle in April to join the peace talks but linked its participation to food aid and an end to U.S. trade sanctions.
Political analysts say Pyongyang has agreed to join the four-way talks in a policy shift designed to hold the reclusive state together.
They say that with famine and a ruined economy, the Stalinist government needs to repair its relationship with Western countries who could provide much-needed assistance.
Nevertheless, the Monday talks opened with North Korea wanting more commitments for food aid, according to a South Korean official.

"North Korea wanted us to commit a specific amount of food aid before they would come to the preparatory talks ... and we were trying to delink the food and the four-party talks," delegate Yu Myung Hwan of the South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs told reporters during a lunch break.
